name: PARAGUAY

flag.title: Tri-sided wonder
flag.note: Only flag with a unique design on each side

lead: Tucked in the heart of South America, Paraguay has no sea but plenty of surprises. A river divides it: green farmland to the east, vast dry Chaco to the west. Almost everyone speaks two languages — Spanish and Guaraní — and shares cold herbal tea from the same cup. The colossal Itaipu Dam powers the whole country from water alone.
geo: The Paraguay River cuts the country in half. To the east lies the Oriental region — green, hilly, home to most people. Farmers grow soya beans on rich red soil; the Paraná River marks the border with Brazil and Argentina.

To the west sprawls the Gran Chaco — South America’s vast wild plain. Thorny forests and wetlands bake in fierce heat. It covers 60% of the land yet holds fewer people than a small town. The Pantanal wetlands touch the far north.
animals: The giant anteater roams the Chaco on its knuckles, slurping 35,000 ants a day through a tube-like snout. Jaguars pad through the night and tapirs crash through riverside undergrowth near the rivers.

The capybara — world’s largest rodent, as big as a labrador — wallows happily in Paraguay’s wetlands. Over 500 bird species fill the air, including the brilliant hyacinth macaw and the towering jabiru stork.
culture: Paraguay is one of the only countries where nearly everyone speaks an indigenous language daily. Guaraní rings out in markets, songs, and jokes. The Paraguayan harp — light and portable — plays at every celebration alongside guitar.

Sharing tereré (ice-cold yerba mate) is as important as a handshake. Friends pass the same gourd in a circle; UNESCO lists it as Intangible Heritage. Delicate lace called ñandutí, meaning ‘spider web’, is another beloved Paraguayan craft.
history: Paraguay broke from Spain on 14 May 1811 without a shot fired. But the War of the Triple Alliance (1864–70) against Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay was catastrophic: it killed roughly half the population and nearly 90% of adult men.

The country rebuilt, then beat Bolivia in the Chaco War (1932–35), winning most of the disputed wilderness. A long dictatorship under Stroessner (1954–89) ended peacefully; democracy has held ever since.
wows: Paraguay’s flag is the only one worldwide with a different emblem each side — star on front, lion on back.
Itaipu Dam set a 2016 world record: 103 terawatt-hours of hydro power in a single year.
Landlocked but mighty: Paraguay has the largest navy of any country with no coastline.
Pistol duelling is technically still legal here — as long as both duelists are registered blood donors.
Paraguay set a Guinness record for the world’s largest barbecue, cooking for around 30,000 people.
About 90% of Paraguayans blend Spanish and Guaraní mid-sentence in a daily mix called Jopará.
Paraguay generates nearly 100% of its electricity from water, one of the cleanest grids on Earth.

myths.fact: The eastern half is lush with rolling hills and river valleys; only the western Chaco is arid — and even it floods into wetland life during the rains.
Guaraní thrives — spoken daily by over 90% of Paraguayans regardless of wealth or background, making it one of the healthiest indigenous languages anywhere.
